title: What Are We Protecting When We Blame Others
author: Camilo Zambrano
summary: Camilo Zambrano explores victim mentality as a form of what he calls drift, the gap between what we say we value and how we behave under stress. Opening with a broken laptop that tempted him to stop writing, and a Madrid conversation with his aunt Teresa who told him he placed blame everywhere but looked inward, he argues that responsibility begins with owning your part. He offers three possible childhood pathways to externalizing blame, namely overly strict upbringing, anxious or controlling upbringing, and overindulgence without boundaries, and notes that toxic workplaces can trigger the same response as a trauma reaction. He then applies his return loop of noticing, regulating, choosing and acting, starting with building the habit of noticing through mindfulness and physical cues, followed by pausing to regulate before acting.
points: Zambrano frames blame as a protective move against shame or helplessness, so the useful question is what the blame is shielding rather than who is at fault.
He sketches three childhood routes to a victim mentality: strictness that breeds powerlessness, apprehension that breeds dependence, and lack of boundaries that breeds entitlement.
A toxic workplace can create the same pattern in an adult, making fair feedback in a later job feel like another unfair attack.
Because drift is data, the remedy is to manage rather than eliminate it by training the return loop in parts, starting with noticing physical cues such as a clenched jaw or racing thoughts.
Regulation means pausing to mitigate before investigating, the way one teaches a child to cope with feelings rather than simply stop crying.
quotes: Think about it: how much of your behavior has come, at some point, from the idea that it was someone else’s fault or they did it first?
I have noticed that when you talk, you place the blame everywhere around you, but you forget to look inside. When will you realize that you have to own your part to make a change?
Externalizing the blame helps remove the fear of not being enough for a world that demands more.
Externalizing the blame can then become a way to protect ourselves from the shame we associate with inaction.
When you feel entitled to your actions, then all of a sudden there are no rules that need to be followed. If you face consequences for not following them, it’s their fault, not yours.
People can experience and feel harm without being responsible for causing it; our role is to manage our behavior whether we are responsible or not, and that’s what we’ll see next.
In this newsletter, we talk about drift not as something you need to eliminate, but as something you need to manage. The question then is: How can we manage this?
We don’t want to eliminate it, because eliminating it is a futile game. We want to make sure that if we see ourselves going in that direction, we return as fast as we can.
So we stop and assess. Mitigate first, then investigate. Look for ways to calm yourself down, to bring yourself toward a baseline, and then try to understand what’s behind all of that.
